title: Did Shakespeare write all his plays?

entries.note: Born in 1564 and died on his birthday, 23 April, in 1616; wrote about 40 plays and 154 sonnets, and is credited with about 1,700 words.
Collection of 36 of Shakespeare's plays compiled by friends from sources like actors' copies; no plays in his own hand survive.
Lost play, the counterpart to Love's Labour's Lost, though it may simply have been the original title of As You Like It.
Lost play Shakespeare wrote together with [[see:John Fletcher]], which brings his total to about 41.
Shakespeare's co-writer on the lost play [[see:Cardenio]].
First found in its modern sense in Shakespeare, though the word circumstance already existed with a different meaning.
Existed before Shakespeare, but his works have the first known use in today's sense.
Used by Shakespeare in A Midsummer Night's Dream to mean room in a bed; a 1600 translation already has the modern sense, then usually [[see:bed chamber]].
Character in A Midsummer Night's Dream who asks [[see:Hermia]] for bedroom, trying to cuddle up to her in the forest.
The woman [[see:Lysander]] asks for bedroom in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
The more common word for a [[see:bedroom]] at the time, but it didn't fit Shakespeare's metre.
Shakespeare used it where people said [[see:dawning]], probably cutting a syllable to fit the iambic pentameter.
The usual word for sunrise before Shakespeare used the shorter [[see:dawn]].
Back-formed from [[from:negotiation]]; its first known instance is in Shakespeare.
Back-formed from [[from:metamorphosis]]; its first known instance is in Shakespeare.
First found in Shakespeare, though [[see:assassin]] is older and [[see:assassinate]] probably existed at the same time.
Older than [[see:assassination]], which is first found in Shakespeare.
Probably existed at the same time as Shakespeare's [[see:assassination]].
Coined by Shakespeare by dropping the ending of [[from:grovelling]], which he misunderstood; it means to lie face down or prostrate yourself.
An adverb meaning face down, made with a dialect -ling ending and recorded in 1542; it gave [[gave:grovel]].
Often credited to Shakespeare (Othello, The Tempest), adapted from a Middle English noun and the verb [[from:hinten]], to seize; a small graspable bit of information.
Credited to Shakespeare, though the verb goes back to Old English [[from:cyssan]]; Rob thinks someone must have said kissing before him.
Thought to have been coined by Shakespeare.
Thought to have been coined by Shakespeare.
Shakespeare is credited with being the first to import it from French.
Shakespeare is credited with being the first to import it, from Italian [[from:bandito]].
First used by Shakespeare, who made the noun [[from:gloom]] into an adjective; some sources say it already existed in Scottish varieties.
First recorded in Shakespeare, though the Middle English verb [[from:swag]] already meant to sway.
One of countless words Shakespeare formed by adding or removing affixes.
A multi-toothed farm tool dragged over soil; Hamlet's 'harrow up thy soul' first used it figuratively, which gives today's harrowing.
Shakespeare was the first to use it to mean something other than coins.
A compound of lack and lustre, first recorded in As You Like It describing tired or dull eyes; to Rob's surprise, it just means lacking lustre.
Like [[see:lacklustre]], a compound Rob never saw through: a thing that wards, or protects, your robes.
Another compound, like [[see:lacklustre]], whose parts people tend not to notice.
One of Shakespeare's many compounds with lack, alongside [[see:lack-beard]] and [[see:lack-brain]].
One of Shakespeare's recurring compounds with lack.
One of Shakespeare's recurring compounds with lack.

entries.term: thou hast no more brain than I have in mine elbows
entries.note: Jess's favourite Shakespearean insult, from Troilus and Cressida.
The character behind many of the most famous insults, launched at others in the history plays.
A bolting hutch is a bin for sifting flour from bran, so the target is something that collects beastliness.
Falstaff's insult; dropsy is an older informal term for a swelling of bodily fluids.
A bombard was a medieval cannon used to hurl large stones.
A Shakespearean insult that Jess finds unsurprising.
Jess pictures a trunk sloshing with bodily humours.
One of Jess's favourite Shakespearean insults.
One of Jess's favourite Shakespearean insults.
One of Jess's favourite Shakespearean insults.
One of Jess's favourite Shakespearean insults.
One of Jess's favourite Shakespearean insults.
One of Jess's favourite Shakespearean insults.
One of Jess's favourite Shakespearean insults, usually delivered as part of a volley.
A sport of trading poetic insults, an original rap battle that long predates Shakespeare; covered in their insults episode.
First found in Macbeth, about a whole family murdered at once like chicks taken by a swooping bird; often turned into the eggcorn [[see:one foul swoop]].
Means cruel, vicious or fierce, as in [[see:fell beast]]; related to [[same-root:felon]], unrelated to the past tense of [[unrelated:fall]].
Uses the same [[see:fell]], meaning cruel or fierce, as one fell swoop.
Related to [[same-root:fell]], meaning cruel or fierce.
Felling a tree, related to fall, may have caused folk-etymological overlap with [[see:fell]].
A common eggcorn of [[see:one fell swoop]], heard even on television, perhaps influenced by [[see:murder most foul]].
Comes up often in the plays, which may explain the eggcorn [[see:one foul swoop]].
An idiom from Romeo and Juliet.
Another idiom from Shakespeare.
Sounds modern, but comes from 'let the world slide' in The Taming of the Shrew, meaning let things take their course.
Sounds almost bureaucratic, but comes from King Lear.
From [[see:The Tempest]], where Prospero's actors are spirits that melted into thin air.
Also first found in [[see:The Tempest]].
A genuine Shakespeare creation, a story he wrote from start to finish rather than adapting one; Jess likes its adaptations.
Jess's pick: horny, zany and still hilarious, like a modern sitcom; it has the [[see:bedroom]] passage.
Probably Rob's favourite play, mainly for [[see:Malvolio]] strutting around making a fool of himself.
The [[see:Twelfth Night]] character who makes a complete fool of himself.
Gave Jess nightmares: obscenely bloody and depraved, with people baked into pies; hard to believe the author of As You Like It wrote it.
Considered worse than Titus Andronicus, perhaps for its kill count; Jess thinks its witch scenes have a different style, possibly [[see:Christopher Marlowe]]'s.
Doubts that grew from the mid-1800s, which Rob calls largely classist; both hosts credit Shakespeare while allowing for collaboration.
An Oxbridge-educated candidate in the authorship question; Jess wonders whether he wrote Macbeth's witch scenes.
Shakespeare's illiterate father, a glove maker, local politician and notorious wheeler-dealer.
An Oxbridge-educated candidate in the [[see:Shakespeare authorship question]].
An Oxbridge-educated candidate in the [[see:Shakespeare authorship question]].
An Oxbridge-educated candidate in the [[see:Shakespeare authorship question]], from Derby, where Rob is recording.
Another phrase from Shakespeare, which Rob slips in about the authorship question.
A Shakespeare original; it meant 'take it or leave it' or hit or miss, rather than rubbing elbows.
The biscuit, which Rob calls the best biscuit, brought up as what [[see:hobnob]] really means.
From Love's Labour's Lost: a real Latin word for the state of being able to achieve honours, used there for cheeky effect.
Compared with [[see:honorificabilitudinitatibus]] as a long word with a specific usage.
A cannibal, used humorously in The Merry Wives of Windsor; from anthropo-, person, and [[from:-phage]], something that eats.
The form Jess has seen more recently, another word for cannibals, related to [[same-root:anthropophaginian]].
Made into an idler, made lazy; used in The Two Gentlemen of Verona.
Shakespeare's term for a lazy person.
From Hamlet: having your face covered or muffled, though there it probably refers to a veil.
The excitement of a successful beginning, from being fleshed; Rob thinks it sounds like something zombies do.
A trouble, disturbance or commotion, from Middle French for a confused mess and probably ultimately Italian; reminds Jess of [[see:turmoil]].
Jess thinks it may overlap in sense with [[see:garboil]].
